message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and a move‑in inspection sheet.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds any portion. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs that affect health or safety must be made promptly. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may:
 • Withhold rent (after giving notice),
 • Make the repair yourself and deduct the cost from rent,
 • File a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local code enforcement. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (not punitive). | • Keep receipts or bank records.
• If you’re late, communicate with the landlord and negotiate a payment plan. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies.
• “Reasonable notice” means a written notice stating the purpose, date, and time of entry. | • Keep a log of all entries.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint or seek a court order. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • Report violations to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: The landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least **30 days** before the lease ends. | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail) and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the **Texas Property Code** eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease violation).
• If you contest, you can file a **motion to dismiss** or a **counter‑claim** in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend all court hearings.
• Seek legal aid if you cannot afford an attorney. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, provided you keep receipts and the cost is reasonable. | • Document the defect, notify the landlord, and keep all receipts. | | **Rent Control & Caps** | • Texas has **no statewide rent‑control laws**. Landlords can increase rent at the end of a lease term, but must give proper notice (usually 30 days). | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the systems. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Insurance** | • Tenants are not required by law to carry renter’s insurance, but it’s highly recommended to protect personal property. | • Purchase a policy that covers theft, fire, and liability. | | **Legal Resources** | • **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** – handles housing complaints.
• **Texas Legal Services Center** – free legal help for low‑income residents.
• **Local tenant unions** – often provide workshops and support. | • Contact TDHCA or local legal aid for specific disputes. | --- #### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Read the Lease Thoroughly** – Pay attention to security deposit limits, notice periods, and repair responsibilities. 2. **Document the Condition** – Take photos or videos of the unit and keep a signed move‑in inspection sheet. 3. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections. 4. **Keep Records** – Maintain copies of all communications, receipts, and notices. #### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Next Step | |-------|------------|-----------| | Landlord refuses to make repairs | Send a written notice (email + certified mail) | File a complaint with TDHCA or local code enforcement | | Unlawful eviction notice | Respond in writing, request a hearing | File a motion to dismiss in district court | | Discrimination claim | File a complaint with HUD or Texas Commission on Human Rights | Seek legal representation | --- **Bottom Line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, privacy, fair notice for entry, and protection against discrimination. If a landlord violates these rights, you can use written notices, repair‑and‑deduct, or legal action to enforce them. Always keep documentation and seek professional help if the situation escalates.
